prompt:
Let $n>k$ and let $A_1,\ldots,A_k$ be real $n\times n$ matrices of rank $n-1$. Prove that
$$A_1\cdot\ldots\cdot A_k\neq0 .$$
answer: Kernels add up at most: $\dim\ker(AB)\le\dim\ker A+\dim\ker B$, so $\dim\ker(A_1\cdots A_k)\le k<n$ and the product has rank $\ge n-k\ge1$.

solutions.title: Kernel dimensions are subadditive
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** For $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$: $\dim\ker(AB)\le\dim\ker A+\dim\ker B$.

*Proof.* $B$ maps $\ker(AB)$ into $\ker A$ (if $ABv=0$ then $Bv\in\ker A$). The kernel of this restricted map $\ker(AB)\to\ker A$ is $\ker(AB)\cap\ker B=\ker B$. By rank–nullity for the restriction,
$$\dim\ker(AB)=\dim\ker B+\dim B(\ker(AB))\le\dim\ker B+\dim\ker A.\qquad\square$$

By induction on $k$, $\dim\ker(A_1A_2\cdots A_k)\le\sum_{i=1}^k\dim\ker A_i$. Each $A_i$ has rank $n-1$, so $\dim\ker A_i=1$, and
$$\dim\ker(A_1\cdots A_k)\le k<n .$$
Hence the kernel of $A_1\cdots A_k$ is not all of $\mathbb R^n$, i.e. $\operatorname{rank}(A_1\cdots A_k)\ge n-k\ge1$ and $A_1\cdots A_k\ne0$. (Equivalently, this is Sylvester's inequality $\operatorname{rank}(AB)\ge\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B-n$ applied $k-1$ times.) ∎

solutions.title: Images shrink by at most one dimension
solutions.body:
Think of the product as $v\mapsto A_1(A_2(\cdots(A_kv)))$. Let $W_k=\operatorname{Im}A_k$, of dimension $n-1$, and $W_{i}=A_i(W_{i+1})$ for $i<k$. For any subspace $W$, the restriction $A_i|_W$ has kernel $W\cap\ker A_i$ of dimension at most $1$, so $\dim A_i(W)\ge\dim W-1$. Hence
$$\dim\operatorname{Im}(A_1\cdots A_k)=\dim W_1\ge(n-1)-(k-1)=n-k\ge1,$$
so the product is not the zero matrix. ∎

prompt:
Let $k$ be a positive integer. Compute
$$\sum_{n_1=1}^\infty\sum_{n_2=1}^\infty\cdots\sum_{n_k=1}^\infty\frac{1}{n_1n_2\cdots n_k\,(n_1+\cdots+n_k+1)} .$$

solutions.title: Integral representation
solutions.body:
**Answer: $k!$.**

All terms are positive, so by Tonelli's theorem sums and integrals may be interchanged freely. Using $\frac1{N+1}=\int_0^1x^N\,dx$ with $N=n_1+\dots+n_k$:
$$S=\sum_{n_1,\dots,n_k\ge1}\frac{1}{n_1\cdots n_k}\int_0^1x^{n_1+\dots+n_k}\,dx=\int_0^1\prod_{i=1}^k\left(\sum_{n_i\ge1}\frac{x^{n_i}}{n_i}\right)dx=\int_0^1\big(-\ln(1-x)\big)^k\,dx,$$
since $\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{x^n}{n}=-\ln(1-x)$ for $0\le x<1$. Substitute $1-x=e^{-u}$ ($u\in[0,\infty)$, $dx=e^{-u}du$):
$$S=\int_0^\infty u^ke^{-u}\,du=\Gamma(k+1)=k! .$$
∎

solutions.title: Induction via a recursion
solutions.body:
Let $S_k(m)=\sum_{n_1,\dots,n_k\ge1}\frac{1}{n_1\cdots n_k(n_1+\dots+n_k+m)}$ for real $m>0$; we want $S_k(1)$. The same integral idea, $\frac1{N+m}=\int_0^1x^{N+m-1}dx$, gives
$$S_k(m)=\int_0^1x^{m-1}(-\ln(1-x))^k\,dx .$$
For $m=1$ this is $\int_0^1(-\ln(1-x))^kdx=\int_0^1(-\ln y)^kdy$ (with $y=1-x$). Integrating by parts with $I_k=\int_0^1(-\ln y)^k\,dy$:
$$I_k=\Big[y(-\ln y)^k\Big]_0^1+k\int_0^1(-\ln y)^{k-1}dy=kI_{k-1},$$
since $y(-\ln y)^k\to0$ as $y\to0^+$. With $I_0=1$ we get $I_k=k!$. (Check: for $k=1$, $\sum_n\frac1{n(n+1)}=1$.) **Answer: $k!$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $p$ and $q$ be complex polynomials with $\deg p>\deg q$ and let $f(z)=\dfrac{p(z)}{q(z)}$. Suppose that all roots of $p$ lie inside the unit circle $|z|=1$ and that all roots of $q$ lie outside the unit circle. Prove that
$$\max_{|z|=1}|f'(z)|>\frac{\deg p-\deg q}{2}\max_{|z|=1}|f(z)| .$$
answer: At a point $z_0$ of the unit circle where $|f|$ is maximal, $\left|\frac{z_0f'(z_0)}{f(z_0)}\right|\ge\operatorname{Re}\sum_k\frac{z_0}{z_0-c_k}-\operatorname{Re}\sum_l\frac{z_0}{z_0-d_l}>\frac{n_1}2-\frac{n_2}2$, because $\operatorname{Re}\frac1{1-w}>\frac12\iff|w|<1$.

solutions.title: Logarithmic derivative at the maximum point
solutions.body:
Let $n_1=\deg p$, $n_2=\deg q$, $p(z)=a\prod_{k=1}^{n_1}(z-c_k)$, $q(z)=b\prod_{l=1}^{n_2}(z-d_l)$ with $|c_k|<1<|d_l|$. Then $f$ is holomorphic and nonzero on a neighbourhood of the unit circle.

**Key fact.** For a complex $w\ne1$,
$$\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{1-w}=\frac{\operatorname{Re}(1-\bar w)}{|1-w|^2}=\frac{1-\operatorname{Re}w}{1-2\operatorname{Re}w+|w|^2},$$
so $\operatorname{Re}\frac1{1-w}>\frac12\iff 2-2\operatorname{Re}w>1-2\operatorname{Re}w+|w|^2\iff|w|<1$. Likewise $\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{1-w}<\frac12\iff|w|>1$.

**At the maximum.** Choose $z_0$ with $|z_0|=1$ and $|f(z_0)|=\max_{|z|=1}|f|>0$. The logarithmic derivative is
$$\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n_1}\frac1{z-c_k}-\sum_{l=1}^{n_2}\frac1{z-d_l},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \frac{z_0f'(z_0)}{f(z_0)}=\sum_k\frac{1}{1-c_k/z_0}-\sum_l\frac1{1-d_l/z_0}.$$
Here $|c_k/z_0|=|c_k|<1$ and $|d_l/z_0|>1$, so by the key fact
$$\left|\frac{f'(z_0)}{f(z_0)}\right|=\left|\frac{z_0f'(z_0)}{f(z_0)}\right|\ge\operatorname{Re}\frac{z_0f'(z_0)}{f(z_0)}>\frac{n_1}2-\frac{n_2}2 .$$
(The sum over $k$ is nonempty since $n_1>n_2\ge0$, which makes the inequality strict.) Therefore
$$\max_{|z|=1}|f'(z)|\ge|f'(z_0)|>\frac{n_1-n_2}{2}\,|f(z_0)|=\frac{\deg p-\deg q}{2}\max_{|z|=1}|f(z)| .\qquad ∎$$

prompt:
Let $\mathbb Q[x]$ denote the vector space over $\mathbb Q$ of polynomials with rational coefficients in one variable $x$. Find all $\mathbb Q$-linear maps $\Phi:\mathbb Q[x]\to\mathbb Q[x]$ such that for any irreducible polynomial $p\in\mathbb Q[x]$ the polynomial $\Phi(p)$ is also irreducible.

(A polynomial $p\in\mathbb Q[x]$ is called irreducible if it is non-constant and the equality $p=q_1q_2$ is impossible for non-constant polynomials $q_1,q_2\in\mathbb Q[x]$.)
answer: Exactly the maps $\Phi(p)(x)=a\,p(bx+c)$ with $a,b,c\in\mathbb Q$, $a,b\ne0$. (Show $\Phi(1)$ is a nonzero constant and $\Phi(x)$ linear, normalise to $\Phi(1)=1$, $\Phi(x)=x$, then prove $\Phi(x^n)=x^n$ by induction using Eisenstein polynomials with a prescribed value.)

solutions.title: Normalise, then induct with Eisenstein's criterion
solutions.body:
**Answer:** $\Phi(p)(x)=a\,p(bx+c)$ with rational $a\ne0$, $b\ne0$, $c$.

**These work.** Such $\Phi$ is linear. If $a\,p(bx+c)=q_1(x)q_2(x)$ with $q_1,q_2$ non-constant, substituting $x\mapsto\frac{x-c}{b}$ gives $p(x)=a^{-1}q_1\!\left(\frac{x-c}b\right)q_2\!\left(\frac{x-c}b\right)$, a factorisation of $p$ into non-constant factors. So $\Phi$ maps irreducible polynomials to irreducible ones.

Now let $\Phi$ be any such map. Recall: an irreducible polynomial with a rational root $x_0$ is divisible by $x-x_0$, hence is linear.

**Lemma 1.** If $f,g\in\mathbb Q[x]$ and $f+cg$ is irreducible for every $c\in\mathbb Q$, then $g=0$, or $f$ is linear (non-constant) and $g$ is a nonzero constant.

*Proof.* Let $g\ne0$. Pick a rational $x_0$ with $g(x_0)\ne0$ and put $c=-f(x_0)/g(x_0)$. Then $f+cg$ is irreducible with root $x_0$, so $f+cg=C(x-x_0)$, $C\ne0$. Pick a rational $x_1\ne x_0$ with $g(x_1)\ne0$ and $c_1=-f(x_1)/g(x_1)$; similarly $f+c_1g=C_1(x-x_1)$. Also $c_1\ne c$, because $(f+cg)(x_1)=C(x_1-x_0)\ne0$. Subtracting, $(c_1-c)g$ has degree $\le1$, so $\deg g\le1$, and then $\deg f\le1$. Write $f=\alpha x+\beta$, $g=\alpha_1x+\beta_1$. Here $\alpha\neq0$ since $f=f+0\cdot g$ is irreducible. If $\alpha_1\ne0$, then $f-\frac{\alpha}{\alpha_1}g$ is constant, not irreducible. So $g=\beta_1\ne0$ is constant. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** $g_0=\Phi(1)$ is a nonzero constant and $g_1=\Phi(x)$ is linear and non-constant.

*Proof.* $x+c$ is irreducible for all $c$, so $g_1+cg_0=\Phi(x+c)$ is irreducible for all $c$. By Lemma 1, either the claim holds or $g_0=0$. Suppose $g_0=0$. For every rational $\alpha$ choose $\beta>\alpha^2/4$; then $x^2+\alpha x+\beta$ has no real root, hence is irreducible, and $\Phi(x^2+\alpha x+\beta)=g_2+\alpha g_1$ (with $g_2=\Phi(x^2)$) is irreducible for every $\alpha$. By Lemma 1, $g_1$ is zero or constant — but $g_1=\Phi(x)$ is irreducible, hence non-constant. Contradiction. $\square$

**Normalisation.** Write $g_0=C\ne0$, $g_1=Ax+B$, $A\ne0$. Let $\sigma(x)=\frac{Cx-B}{A}$ and define $\Psi(p)=C^{-1}\,\Phi(p)\circ\sigma$. It is linear, preserves irreducibility (by the first paragraph), and $\Psi(1)=1$, $\Psi(x)=C^{-1}(A\sigma(x)+B)=x$. We show $\Psi=\mathrm{id}$; then $\Phi(p)=C\,p\circ\sigma^{-1}$, i.e. $\Phi(p)(x)=C\,p\!\left(\frac{A}{C}x+\frac BC\right)$, which has the stated form.

**Induction.** Let $n\ge2$ and assume $\Psi(x^j)=x^j$ for $j<n$. Put $h=\Psi(x^n)-x^n$; by linearity
$$\Psi(f)=f+h\qquad\text{for every monic } f \text{ of degree } n. \tag{$*$}$$
Suppose $h\ne0$; we find a monic irreducible $f$ of degree $n$ with $f+h$ reducible (or constant), contradicting $(*)$.

*Case $n=2$ and $h=-x^2+\alpha x+\beta$.* Take $f=x^2-\alpha x+\gamma$ with $\gamma>\alpha^2/4$ (irreducible). Then $\Psi(f)=\beta+\gamma$ is constant — not irreducible.

*General case.* Choose a rational $x_0$ with $h(x_0)\neq0$. Translating ($x\mapsto x+x_0$ preserves monicity, degree and irreducibility) we may assume $x_0=0$. Let $r=-h(0)=u/v\ne0$ with $u\in\mathbb Z$, $v\in\mathbb Z_{>0}$ coprime. We construct monic irreducible $f$ of degree $n$ with $f(0)=r$; then $f+h$ has the rational root $0$, so it is not irreducible unless it is linear.

Let $L=6uv$ and $M=vL^n/u=6^nu^{n-1}v^{n+1}\in\mathbb Z$ (here $n\ge2$). Since $|M|\ge36$, $M-1$ has a prime divisor $p$, and as $6uv\mid M$, $p\nmid 6uv$; in particular $p\nmid L$, $p\ge5$. Put $N=vL^n-u=u(M-1)$, so $p\mid N$. For integers $s,t$ define
$$f_{s,t}(x)=(x+L)^n-L^n+r+p\,(sx+tx^2)\qquad(t=0\text{ if }n=2).$$
Then $f_{s,t}$ is monic of degree $n$ and $f_{s,t}(0)=r$. In the variable $y=x+L$:
$$f_{s,t}=y^n+p\big(s(y-L)+t(y-L)^2\big)-L^n+\frac uv .$$
All coefficients of $y^1,\dots,y^{n-1}$ are integers divisible by $p$, and the constant term is $\frac{-N+pvL(tL-s)}{v}$. Multiply by $v$ (coprime to $p$): Eisenstein's criterion at $p$ applies to $v f_{s,t}$ provided $p^2\nmid -N+pvL(tL-s)$, i.e. provided
$$tL-s\not\equiv \rho\pmod p,\qquad \rho:=\frac{N}{p}\,(vL)^{-1}\bmod p .$$
For fixed $t$, at most one of $s\in\{0,1\}$ violates this. So for $t=0$ there is $s_0\in\{0,1\}$, and for $t=1$ (when $n\ge3$) there is $s_1\in\{0,1\}$, such that $f_{s_0,0}$ and $f_{s_1,1}$ are irreducible (Eisenstein + Gauss's lemma).

- If $n=2$ (and $h$ not of the special form treated above): $f=f_{s_0,0}$ is monic quadratic, $f+h$ is linear only if $h=-x^2+(\text{linear})$, which was the special case. So $f+h$ has degree $\ne1$ and a root at $0$, hence is not irreducible.
- If $n\ge3$: $f_{s_1,1}-f_{s_0,0}=p x^2+p(s_1-s_0)x$ has degree $2$, so $f_{s_0,0}+h$ and $f_{s_1,1}+h$ cannot both have degree $\le1$. Take $f$ to be one of them for which $f+h$ does not have degree $1$. Then $f+h$ is either constant or of degree $\ge2$ with the rational root $0$; in neither case is it irreducible.

Either way $(*)$ is contradicted. Hence $h=0$, $\Psi(x^n)=x^n$, and by induction and linearity $\Psi=\mathrm{id}$.

**Answer:** exactly the maps $\Phi(p)(x)=a\,p(bx+c)$, $a,b,c\in\mathbb Q$, $a\ne0\ne b$. ∎
